brief_problem: The tray that waits for everyone

runs.text: A concurrent program splits the work into tasks that move forward by turns, and waits for all of them before going on.
The problem
The kiosk kitchen has
three cooks
: one makes
3 juices
of 3 pesos, another
2 sandwiches
of 5 pesos and another
4 fruits
of 2 pesos. The tray is served
only when the three have finished
, and the ticket carries the total value of the tray. Until now, every program did one thing after another.
How do you write a kitchen where the three work at once and the tray waits for all of them?
Try it
Work out the value of the tray and say what has to happen before it is handed over.
27 pesos
. The tray waits for the three to finish, no matter who finishes first.
A new paradigm
A paradigm is a way of organising a program; in imperative programming, the program is a list of orders that change memory.
Until now, every program was a single line of orders: the next one started when the previous one finished.
Concurrent programming
offers another way to organise it.

question.text: what if a program were a team of workers that move forward by turns and wait for each other when needed?

metaphor.text: a kitchen with several cooks and a single stove that they take turns at. It stops holding at one point: a cook can decide alone when to leave the stove; a task gives up its turn only when it waits for something.

history.text: in 1965, Edsger Dijkstra published how to coordinate processes that share resources. In 1978, Tony Hoare described processes that communicate by sending each other messages, the idea used by the next lesson.

cost.text: you have to think about what can happen at once and what has to wait; some errors only show up with certain turns.

runs.text: Concurrency
is that possibility: that several parts of a program move forward without waiting for the previous one to finish completely.
Understand and plan

entries.text: What goes in and what comes out?
Three orders with price and amount go in; the value of the tray comes out.
The report card of Part II: three equal calculations with different data.
What can happen at once and what has to wait?
The three dishes are independent; the tray waits for the three.

todas terminaron

runs.text: The only guaranteed thing is the last line:
comes after the two greetings, because
waits for the two tasks. That Ana greets before Leo is what the engine gives today, but the program does not promise it.
How do they move forward
at once
on a single computer? By turns. The
schedule
is the line of ready tasks: it gives the turn to one, and when that task waits for something, it gives the turn to the next.

caption.text: The schedule with the running task, the ready queue and the suspended ones. When the current one suspends, the head of the queue comes in.

What you learned

points.text: Concurrent programming organises a program into parts that can move forward at once; concurrency is that possibility of moving forward by turns.
A task is a job that is launched so that it moves forward on its own; its scope waits for it before going on.
The schedule shares out the turns among the tasks; a task that waits gives up its turn to another.
